name: Clavicle rotation guide

lead: The clavicle rotation guide is a looksmaxxing topic about changing how the collarbones sit so the shoulder line looks wider, flatter or more level. Shoulders are a large part of the upper-body silhouette, so followers look for ways to improve their appearance beyond building muscle.

Anatomy texts describe the clavicle as a roughly 15 cm S-shaped strut that does rotate along its long axis when the arm is raised. Posture and muscle development change how the shoulders present; no published trial has tested whether a rotation routine permanently changes collarbone position.

paras: Community discussion centres on posture awareness, scapular and shoulder positioning, and training for the muscles around the shoulder girdle, often alongside deltoid and upper-back work.
Posture and mobility work are generally low-risk. Anyone with shoulder pain or an injury is typically directed to a clinician, and forcing joint positions is the main concern in forum discussion.

angle.text: Followers use posture awareness and shoulder-girdle training to change how the collarbones and shoulders sit, aiming for a wider-looking, cleaner shoulder line.

lead: The clavicle rotation guide is a topic in looksmaxxing bone and posture discussion concerning the positioning and rotation of the collarbones to change the line of the shoulders. The aim is a broader-looking, more level shoulder profile.

The clavicle is a slender, S-shaped bone about 15 cm long that links the shoulder blade to the breastbone at the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, and it rotates about its long axis like a key as the arm is raised.[1] Because it forms the bony frame of the shoulders, discussion of shoulder width often starts there.

Published research on shoulder-girdle positioning has examined how alignment changes between lying and standing postures, which shows that position affects measured shoulder geometry.[2] No study has tested a clavicle rotation routine as an appearance intervention.

paras: The clavicle is the only long bone that lies horizontally. Its medial end meets the sternum and its lateral end meets the acromion of the scapula, and it acts as a strut holding the scapula in place so the arm can hang freely.[1] It rotates axially during arm elevation.[1] Clavicle rotation guides draw on this mobility to discuss how shoulder position influences the visual line from neck to shoulder.

The clavicle is the first bone to start ossifying, at the fifth and sixth weeks of gestation, but one of the last to finish, at about 21 to 25 years of age.[1] Its length is fixed by skeletal development, which is why discussion in the community separates bone width from how the shoulders are held and how much muscle covers them.

A study of the shoulder girdle in supine and standing positions reported that three-dimensional alignment changes with body position.[2] This establishes that posture changes shoulder-girdle geometry; it does not address long-term change from a rotation routine, and no clinical trial has evaluated one.
No studies found. A study of shoulder-girdle alignment between supine and standing positions exists as related background research.[2]

Participants discuss shoulders as part of the upper-body silhouette and trade posture and mobility ideas next to shoulder-training advice. Clavicle surgery is a separate topic covered in its own entry.
